HEADLINE HYPOTHESIS
-------------------
Between 1990 and 1996, wealth inequality rose modestly within both white females and white males in the NLS 1979 cohort (n = 3,630 white females, 3,469 white males; zero missing values in either wealth year; negative composite wealth treated as debt and retained). The headline Gini coefficient moved from 0.776 (95% bootstrap CI 0.758–0.793) to 0.782 (95% CI 0.769–0.794) for white females (Δ = +0.006; within-resampling 95% CI on the change −0.015 to +0.024), and from 0.792 (95% CI 0.775–0.807) to 0.798 (95% CI 0.785–0.809) for white males (Δ = +0.005; within-resampling 95% CI on the change −0.010 to +0.024). The direction of rising inequality is corroborated by a clear widening of the bulk-of-distribution metrics: standard deviation rose by $34,875 for white females and $72,747 for white males, while the interquartile range rose by $43,875 (+40%) and $56,655 (+62%) respectively. The top-decile wealth share, in contrast, held essentially flat in both groups (Δ = +0.000 for females; −0.002 for males), indicating that the 1990→1996 increase in overall dispersion was driven by widening of the middle of the distribution (IQR, CV) rather than further concentration at the very top. White males remained slightly more unequal than white females in both years (ΔGini(M–F) = +0.016 in 1990 and +0.016 in 1996); the male–female Gini gap did not change materially, so both groups moved upward in parallel. Findings are robust to (a) winsorization at the 1st/99th percentile (Gini 0.736→0.769 for females, 0.766→0.785 for males), and (b) restricting to ever_jailed = 0 (drops only 12 of 3,630 white females and 57 of 3,469 white males; the ever_jailed=1 subgroup is too small for a stratified comparison).

DATA / METHOD
-------------
Data: /workspace/data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 rows; race ∈ {black, hipanic, white}; subset to white × sex). No imputation was needed (zero missing values in 1990 and 1996 wealth columns). Negatives retained as debt. Outliers retained (no deletion). Metric definition: Lorenz-curve rank-based Gini with n/(n–1) small-sample correction, bounded in [0, 1] and well-defined for net-wealth distributions that include debt. Supporting: std, CV (std/|median|), IQR, P90/P50 (avoids the zero-denominator problem at P10 from the heavy mass at 0 in 1996), top-decile share. Bootstrap: 1,000 iterations, percentile method, 95% CIs.
